To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the random error due instrument noise is a significant component of the total random error for low signal-to-noice ratio data and that the systematic flux bias due to the method used to determine the time lag can be significant for such data.

(i) the method of determining the time lag between concentration and wind measurement is important when analysing noisy data, (ii) systematic bias in noisy data is particularly significant for disjunctions in the flux record, and (iii) the statistical significance of the noisy data can be improved by averaging individual flux measurements, but this requires the use of a prescribed time lag

(i) for low signal-to-noose data sets, the method for identifying the time lag between the wind and concentration signal becomes increasingly important as instrument errors approach sampling errors and (ii) the limit of detection for noisy fluxes can be improved (by a factor of 3-5) through appropriate averaging of individual data, provided systematic biases are eliminated by using a prescribed rather than an automated time lag
In summary, our research is concerned with
quantifying the errors associated with eddy-covairance fluxes and with identifying the sources of these errors.
the analysis of noisy data, which is a common situation in the eddy covariance community.
the analysis of data sets with a high noise-to-signal ratio and with the quantification of the associated uncertainties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the time-lag determination is a crucial step in the eddy-covari- ance analysis, and should not be omitted or replaced by a fixed value, unless it is known that the time lag does in fact not fluctuate over time.
the use of prescribed time lags is the best way to deal with low signal-to noise data, but only if the time lag is not changing significantly over time.
the time lag of a noisy signal should not be identified by the cross-covariances of the two signals, as the resulting bias can be substantial.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

for low signal-to-noice data, the use of prescribed time lags is recommended and should be accompanied by an estimate of the random flux error due to instrument uncertainties, which can then be added to the random error due the sampling error.
the use of a prescribed time lag, rather than the maximum in the auto-covariance function, is essential for the analysis of noisy flux data.
the time-lag identification is crucial for low signal-to-noice ratio measurements and that a prescribed time lag is the best option to avoid biases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
when analysing noisy data, the time-lag determination is of utmost importance.
the time lag of a low signal-to-noice system should not be determined by the maximum of the cross-covariation function but rather by a prescribed time lag.
the time lag should be determined independently from the fluxes and that the time lag must be constant over the time period used to compute the flux.
